samples.summary: SSRF address pin is silently dropped whenever an egress proxy applies, re-opening DNS rebinding through the proxy's own resolution
samples.evidence: `hopDispatcher()` returns a `ProxyAgent` and never a `pinnedAgent` when `proxyForUrl(target)` matches (image-fetcher.ts:397-409). The file comment and `docs/design/cli.md` both claim "Dropping the pin there costs nothing that was ever held ... under a proxy the CLI performs no connect-time resolution at all." That is only half true: the proxy resolves the name instead, and its answer is not the answer the gate approved. Vector: an attacker who can edit/share a document sets `src=http://rebind.attacker/x` behind a nameserver with ~0s TTL. `assertFetchableImageUrl` (line 316) resolves it to a public address and allows it; the request is then handed to the operator's `http_proxy`, which re-resolves `rebind.attacker` and gets `169.254.169.254` (or an internal host). The proxy fetches it and the bytes are embedded in the PDF/DOCX/PPTX the victim reads — exactly the SSRF this gate exists to stop, on precisely the machines (corporate, proxy-only egress) where internal targets are most valuable. The gate's own resolution is not authoritative for the proxied hop, so nothing else constrains it. Mitigation would be to pass the gate's approved address as the connect target (or refuse to proxy names whose gate-time and request-time identity cannot be tied), rather than asserting the risk is nil.

samples.summary: Web GitHub OAuth flow forwards no `state`, and passport does not validate one — OAuth login-CSRF / session fixation on the browser path; the `csrf` token CliAuthStore mints is never verified anywhere
samples.evidence: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` sets `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` is present (github.strategy.ts:59-62), i.e. only for `mode=cli`. The constructor `super({...})` (lines 43-49) passes no `state: true` and no `store`, so passport-oauth2 installs a `NullStore` whose `verify` always succeeds — no state is generated, sent, or checked for the ordinary web login. `AuthController.githubAuthCallback` then reaches the web branch with `stateToken === undefined` and unconditionally sets session cookies (auth.controller.ts:145-149). Vector: attacker starts GitHub OAuth for their own account, captures the resulting `?code=`, and makes the victim's browser load `GET /auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>`; the backend mints and sets `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` cookies for the attacker's account, so the victim silently works inside the attacker's account (classic OAuth login CSRF / session fixation). `CliAuthStore.createState` generates a per-request `csrf` (cli-auth.store.ts:32) and `consumeState` returns it (line 55), but a repo-wide grep for `csrf` finds no consumer outside the store and its own specs — the intended control was never wired up. Pre-existing rather than introduced here, but this change is the one hardening this exact flow and the diff's own design-doc table claims "OAuth state forgery (CSRF)" is mitigated.

samples.summary: Image-gate server exemption keys only on (port, resolved address), never on hostname, so any attacker-named host resolving to the API server's address on its port is fetched with an attacker-chosen path and Host header
samples.evidence: `mayBeServer` is true whenever `effectivePort(url) === effectivePort(server)` (line 307-308) and the `allowed` filter passes any address in `exempt` unconditionally — `exempt.has(a.toLowerCase()) || (!internalName && !isPrivateAddress(a))` (lines 322-325) — where `exempt` is the set of addresses the configured `--server` resolves to (`serverAddresses`, line 253). The hostname of the image URL is never compared to the server's. Vector: with the documented dev setup `--server http://localhost:3000` (exempt = {127.0.0.1}), a malicious document carries `src=http://evil.attacker.tld:3000/<any path>` whose A record is 127.0.0.1. The private-address check is skipped because the address is in `exempt`, and the CLI issues `GET /<any path>` to 127.0.0.1:3000 with `Host: evil.attacker.tld`, embedding the response bytes into the exported artifact. The same holds for a self-hosted `--server https://wafflebase.corp.internal` (exempt = its internal address), turning the exemption into an attacker-steerable reader of arbitrary paths on the internal API host — including any Host-routed vhost co-located on that address. Tightening to an origin/hostname match (or at least rejecting a name that is not the server's own) closes it without breaking the localhost/127.0.0.1 spelling case the exemption exists for.

samples.summary: The login nonce — the only secret binding the loopback callback — is printed to stderr and passed as browser argv, so anyone who can read the CLI's logs during the 30s window can complete a login fixation
samples.evidence: `runLogin` generates the nonce (line 226) and then prints the full OAuth URL including it: `console.error(`Opening browser: ${oauthUrl}`)` (line 239), where `oauthUrl` embeds both `port` and `nonce` (line 238); it is also handed to `open()` as a process argument (line 197). Everything else in this change treats the nonce as a secret (constant-time compare, `403` on mismatch, `redactUrl` applied to every other URL that reaches stderr). Vector: an attacker who can read the CLI's stderr — a captured CI/agent transcript, a shared terminal recording, another process able to read the browser's cmdline — learns `<port>` and `<nonce>` while the 30s listener is still open, then completes `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>` as *themselves*; the backend echoes the victim's nonce (auth.controller.ts:130-135), the victim's CLI accepts the callback and writes a session for the attacker's account. `docs/tasks/active/20260803-cli-system-exit-code-lessons.md` acknowledges the nonce "does travel in the printed OAuth URL and the browser argv", but neither the CLI README nor `docs/design/cli.md` §8.1 records that the printed URL must be treated as a credential — the design doc presents the binding as unqualified. At minimum the printed URL deserves a "do not share while login is pending" note, and agent-facing capture of that line should be considered secret.

samples.summary: The malformed-URL block message interpolates the raw target instead of `redactUrl(target)`, defeating the redaction applied to every sibling message
samples.evidence: `throw blocked(`Refusing to fetch malformed image URL "${target}".`)` (line 291) is the only message in this file that does not pass the URL through `redactUrl` — every neighbouring throw does (lines 297, 311, 330, 331, 601, 617). `target` on the first hop is `resolveImageUrl(url, opts.serverBase)`, so it can carry userinfo from `--server`/`WAFFLEBASE_SERVER` (`https://user:pass@host/...`), and on a redirect hop it is `new URL(location, target)` which can carry a presigned query string. That string is written verbatim to stderr by `outputError` and lands in CI logs — the exact leak `redactUrl`'s docblock (errors.ts:87-93) says it exists to prevent.

samples.summary: `isPrivateAddress` misses the IPv4-translated `::ffff:0:0/96` prefix and site-local `fec0::/10`
samples.evidence: The IPv4-embedded branch only fires when `words.slice(0,5)` are all zero (line 161), which covers `::ffff:7f00:1` (`words[4]=0`) but not the IPv4-translated form `::ffff:0:7f00:1`, whose expansion is `[0,0,0,0,0xffff,0,0x7f00,1]` — `words[4]=0xffff` so the branch is skipped, and none of the later prefixes match, so `isPrivateAddress('::ffff:0:7f00:1')` returns **false** and 127.0.0.1 is reachable in that spelling on any host that routes `::ffff:0:0/96`. Likewise `fec0::/10` (deprecated site-local) is not covered: `(words[0] & 0xffc0) === 0xfe80` (line 170) is false for `0xfec0`. Reached either via an attacker AAAA record (the address goes straight into `allowed` at line 322 and is then pinned as the connect target) or a bracketed literal in a document `src`. Low routability in practice, but the stated design goal is "in every spelling".

samples.summary: The security-downgrading `--allow-unbound-callback` flag is published in the machine-readable agent schema, where an autonomous agent may select it to clear a failing login
samples.evidence: `registry.ts:48` adds `'--allow-unbound-callback'` to the `login` command's `parameters`. The design doc's own reasoning (docs/design/cli.md, "Nonce-bound login callback") is that the escape hatch must be discoverable "only where an attacker has no say — `wafflebase login --help` and the README" precisely so a failing login cannot steer someone into disabling the binding. The schema registry is described in the same doc as "the agent interface": an agent whose `wafflebase login` times out (which is exactly what a hostile nonce-less callback produces) can enumerate this flag and retry with the binding off, completing the login-fixation the invariant timeout message was designed to prevent. The description text warns, but an agent selecting parameters by name is not a reader an attacker has no say over.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repository. `hopDispatcher` (image-fetcher.ts:393-410) returns a `ProxyAgent` and discards the gate-approved `addresses` whenever `proxyForUrl(target)` is non-null, reaching `pinnedAgent` only on the no-proxy path (line 409). `pinnedAgent` (347-369) is the sole mechanism binding the gate's verdict to the actual connection — it overrides the connector's `lookup` — so on a proxied hop nothing ties gate-time identity to request-time identity. The path is reachable on every image hop: `createImageFetcher` calls `assertFetchableImageUrl` (581) then `hopDispatcher` (582) and passes the dispatcher to `fetchOrThrow` (584-594)/`rawRequest` (595), and `proxyForUrl` (456-473) reads `http_proxy`/`https_proxy`/`all_proxy` from `process.env` by default. An attacker who controls a document `src` plus a ~0s-TTL nameserver can answer the gate's lookup (316) with a public address and the proxy's re-resolution with an internal one, causing the proxy to fetch e.g. 169.254.169.254 and embed the bytes in the exported PDF/DOCX/PPTX — the exact rebinding window the pin was built to close (343-345) and the internal-host case the gate refuses (313-314, 322-333). No guard elsewhere constrains the proxied hop; the doc comment at 381-386 asserts the risk is nil, which makes the gap read as covered. SSRF is squarely in the security lens's lane, so no refutation ground (not-present / already-guarded / out-of-scope) applies.

SameSite=lax (auth.controller.ts:261-268) does not block a top-level GET navigation. In-lane (crypto/auth: missing state/CSRF binding) and blocking at major severity.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as the finding describes. `mayBeServer` is derived solely from a port comparison (image-fetcher.ts:307-308) and the allow-filter short-circuits the private-address check for any address in `exempt` (image-fetcher.ts:322-325), where `exempt` is just the set of addresses the configured `--server` resolves to (image-fetcher.ts:253-264). No hostname or origin comparison exists anywhere on the path: `isInternalHostname` (line 76-84) does not fire for an attacker-registered public name, and `resolveHost` (line 214-239) returns the attacker's A record unchallenged. The vector is demonstrated by an existing test that asserts the behavior as intended: `assertFetchableImageUrl('http://mixed.example:3000/x', http://127.0.0.1:3000, …)` with `mixed.example` -> ['127.0.0.1','10.0.0.5'] resolves to ['127.0.0.1'], i.e. an arbitrary attacker-named host with an arbitrary path is fetched against the API server's address:port, with `Host: mixed.example`, via `pinnedAgent` (line 347-369), and the response bytes are embedded into the exported artifact. No refutation ground applies: not-present fails (lines read as quoted), already-guarded fails (no hostname guard; docs/design/cli.md:891-900 documents the address-only match as deliberate, which is not a guard), and out-of-scope fails since SSRF/unsafe input handling is explicitly in the Security lane. The strongest counter-argument — that the same address:port is already reachable by the server's own name, so the delta is the attacker-controlled Host header and name-independent reach — bears on magnitude, not on whether the weakness is real, so it cannot support refutation.

verdict.reason: All cited code is present verbatim: the login nonce is generated at login.ts:226, embedded in the OAuth URL at login.ts:238, printed unredacted to stderr at login.ts:239, and passed as a process argument to open(url) at login.ts:197 (readable by other local users via ps or /proc/<pid>/cmdline). No guard keeps it off stderr or argv - redactUrl (errors.ts:94) is applied to other URLs but never to oauthUrl. The code's own comments (login.ts:221-225, 229) name the threat model as 'any local process that reaches the callback port', which is exactly the adversary that can read argv, so the disclosure directly weakens the defense this change added. The reviewer's remote-CI-transcript variant is weaker than claimed (the backend redirect at auth.controller.ts:133-134 lands on the attacker's own loopback, so a purely remote reader cannot reach the victim's listener), but the local other-uid argv/stderr vector stands and yields login fixation within the 30s window (login.ts:355). mergedFrom.summary: `--allow-unbound-callback` accepts a nonce-less callback from any local origin with no compensating check

finding.summary: An attacker-injected nonce-less callback steers the CLI into recommending `--allow-unbound-callback`, downgrading the login binding
finding.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set by ANY `/callback?code=…` request that omits `nonce` (login.ts:355-356) — the loopback listener is reachable by any local process and by any web page that guesses the port, which is the exact adversary the nonce exists to stop. On timeout the CLI then reports `'Login callback arrived without the expected nonce — the server predates nonce-bound CLI login. … re-run `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback` to accept it anyway.'` (login.ts:417-421). Attack chain: (1) attacker completes GitHub OAuth in their own browser against `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=P`, capturing a valid `code` bound to the ATTACKER's account (the backend hands the code to whoever drove the flow — auth.controller.ts:126); (2) a hostile page in the victim's browser issues `` with no nonce — refused, but it flips `sawUnboundCallback`; (3) the CLI times out and tells the victim the SERVER is at fault and to re-run with `--allow-unbound-callback`; (4) on the re-run, `nonce === null && allowUnbound` (login.ts:351) accepts the attacker's replayed nonce-less callback, and `fetchLoginSession` writes the attacker's tokens to `~/.wafflebase/session.json` (login.ts:248-258). Result: login/session fixation — the victim's subsequent CLI writes land in the attacker's workspace. The failure diagnostic must not be attacker-controllable; distinguish 'server never echoed a nonce' from 'someone injected a callback' (e.g. only trust the absent-nonce signal when it correlates with the state the CLI itself started, or drop the flag recommendation from the message).

verdict.reason: The finding's mechanism is not present in this tree. There is no `sawUnboundCallback` flag: login.ts:354-355 are `allowUnbound`/`timeoutMs` reads from caller options, not request-settable state, and the nonce-less branch at login.ts:388-400 returns 403 without recording anything. The timeout handler at login.ts:447-476 emits a single invariant message, 'Login timed out. Try again with `wafflebase login`.', which contains neither `--allow-unbound-callback` nor 'predates' — the quoted evidence string does not exist in the file. The comment at login.ts:450-467 states this steering message was deliberately removed for exactly the fixation reason the finding describes, and test/login.test.ts:226-249 is a regression test that injects a nonce-less callback and asserts the resulting error does NOT match /--allow-unbound-callback/ or /predates/. Step (3) of the attack chain (CLI recommends the downgrade flag) therefore cannot occur, breaking the chain. The remaining behaviour — accepting a nonce-less callback only when the operator explicitly passes the flag (login.ts:389, warned at login.ts:227-231) — is an explicit documented opt-out, not the reported defect.
